title: Curriculum
subtitle: Grammar that unlocks the words you already read

lessons.title: 1. The three kinds of words
lessons.concept: Every Arabic word is a noun (اسم), a verb (فعل), or a particle (حرف).
lessons.explanation: Classical grammar (naḥw) begins with one division: speech is made of nouns, verbs, and particles. A noun (ism) names a thing, person, or quality and carries no time. A verb (fiʿl) is an action tied to a time (past, present, command). A particle (ḥarf) has no meaning on its own — it links other words (like 'in', 'and', 'to'). Learn to sort every word into one of these three and grammar starts to fall into place.
keyPoints: Ism (noun): الله، رب، رحمن — names and qualities, no time.
Fiʿl (verb): نَعْبُدُ (we worship), اهْدِنَا (guide us) — actions with time.
Ḥarf (particle): بِ (in), وَ (and), مِنْ (from) — connectors with no standalone meaning.

quiz.q: What kind of word is نَعْبُدُ ('we worship')?
quiz.explanation: It is an action tied to a time (present tense) — a verb.
It has no meaning by itself and only links words — a particle (ḥarf).

lessons.title: 2. The definite article (al-)
lessons.concept: ال (al-) attached to the front of a noun makes it 'the'.
lessons.explanation: Arabic has no separate word for 'the' — it prefixes ال onto the noun. الْحَمْدُ = 'the praise'. When ال meets a 'sun letter' (like ر, ش, س), the ل assimilates and the next letter doubles: الرَّحْمَٰن is read 'ar-raḥmān', not 'al-raḥmān'. A noun with ال is definite (maʿrifah); without it, it is indefinite (nakirah) and often ends in tanwīn (-un/-in/-an).
keyPoints: ال = 'the'; it attaches directly to the noun.
Sun letters double after ال: الشَّمْس → 'ash-shams'.

quiz.q: Why is الرَّحْمَٰن pronounced 'ar-raḥmān' and not 'al-raḥmān'?
options: ر is a sun letter, so ل assimilates and ر doubles
Because it is a name of Allah
quiz.explanation: ر is a sun letter; the ل of ال assimilates into it and the following letter is doubled (shaddah).

lessons.title: 3. Possession (Iḍāfah): muḍāf & muḍāf ilayh
lessons.concept: Two nouns joined to mean 'the X of Y' — رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ = 'Lord of the worlds'.
lessons.explanation: Iḍāfah chains two nouns to show possession or relationship. The first noun (muḍāf) takes NO ال and NO tanwīn; the second noun (muḍāf ilayh) is always genitive (majrūr, -i). So رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ = 'Lord of the worlds': رَبِّ is muḍāf, الْعَالَمِينَ is muḍāf ilayh. Spotting iḍāfah is one of the fastest ways to read Qurʾanic phrases correctly.
keyPoints: Muḍāf (1st noun): no ال, no tanwīn.

examples.translation: Master of the Day of Judgment

quiz.q: In رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ, which word is the muḍāf ilayh (genitive second noun)?
quiz.explanation: الْعَالَمِينَ is the second noun and is majrūr — the muḍāf ilayh. رَبِّ is the muḍāf.

lessons.title: 4. Preposition + genitive (Jār & Majrūr)
lessons.concept: A preposition pulls the following noun into the genitive case (-i).
lessons.explanation: Certain particles — بِ (in/with), لِ (to/for), مِنْ (from), فِي (in), عَلَىٰ (on) — are 'jārr' (pullers): the noun after them must be majrūr (genitive). بِسْمِ = بِ + اسْمِ ('in the name'); لِلَّهِ = لِ + اللَّهِ ('to Allah'). Together the preposition and its noun form a 'jār-majrūr' phrase, which usually attaches to a verb or stands as a predicate.
keyPoints: Prepositions: بِ، لِ، مِنْ، فِي، عَلَىٰ، إِلَىٰ، عَنْ.
The noun after them is genitive (majrūr, ends -i / -in).
بِ + اسْم = بِسْم; لِ + الله = لله.

quiz.q: After the preposition لِ, what case is the noun in?
quiz.explanation: Prepositions put the following noun in the genitive (majrūr): لِلَّهِ ends in -i.

lessons.title: 5. Roots & patterns (intro to ṣarf)
lessons.concept: Most Arabic words come from a 3-letter root poured into a pattern.
lessons.explanation: Arabic vocabulary is built from triliteral roots — a sequence of (usually three) consonants carrying a core meaning. The root ح-م-د means 'praise'. Pour it into different patterns and you get a family: الْحَمْد (the praise), حَمِدَ (he praised), مَحْمُود (praiseworthy), مُحَمَّد (the much-praised one), حَمِيد (praiseworthy). Learn to extract the root from any word and you unlock its whole family at once — this is the engine of ṣarf.
keyPoints: Root = the bare consonants (e.g. ح م د).
Pattern = the vowels/extra letters added around the root.
Same root → related meanings across many words.

examples.note: root ع ب د → also عَبْد 'servant', عِبَادَة 'worship'
root ع و ن, Form X → also مَعُونَة 'aid', إِعَانَة 'assistance'

quiz.q: What is the root of نَعْبُدُ ('we worship')?
quiz.explanation: The core consonants are ع-ب-د ('to worship/serve') — also seen in عَبْد (servant) and عِبَادَة (worship).

lessons.title: 6. Case endings & basic iʿrāb
lessons.concept: The short vowel on a word's end shows its job in the sentence.
lessons.explanation: Iʿrāb is the system of case endings that signals a word's grammatical role. The three cases are: marfūʿ (nominative, -u) for the subject; manṣūb (accusative, -a) for the object; majrūr (genitive, -i) after prepositions and in iḍāfah. الْحَمْدُ ends in -u because it is the subject (mubtadaʾ); لِلَّهِ ends in -i because it follows a preposition. The endings are why vocalization (tashkīl) matters — they carry grammar, not just sound.
keyPoints: Majrūr (-i): after prepositions and as muḍāf ilayh.
Use the Reader's iʿrāb mode to parse whole ayahs interactively.

quiz.q: الصِّرَاطَ in 'guide us to the straight path' ends in -a. What is its role?
quiz.explanation: The -a ending is manṣūb (accusative) — here it is the object of the verb 'guide'.
